newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Bomb may have killed man tied to Slovak abduction.
newsitem.headline: Bomb may have killed man tied to Slovak abduction.

text.p: The Slovak Interior Ministry said on Thursday that a blast which killed an ex-policeman linked to the kidnapping of President Michal Kovac's son appeared to have been caused by an explosive and not a gas leak as originally suggested.
Robert Remias died when the propane gas-fuelled car he was driving exploded and burst into flames on the outskirts of Bratislava on April 29.
His death provoked uproar following suggestions that last year's kidnapping of Michal Kovac Junior to Austria was linked to a bitter feud between the president and Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar.
Initial police reports said the blast could have been due to a leak in the propane circuit. But the Interior Ministry, whose head was fired last month, said this had changed.
"The latest police reports indicate that the blast was caused by an unidentified explosive set up in the car," said Jan Kostov, head of the ministry's investigation department.
But Kostov told Reuters: "The version about the bomb has not yet been 100 percent proved."
The opposition says it suspects Remias was assassinated, suggesting his death was linked to his connections with a former member of the SIS state intelligence service.

The former agent, who has gone into hiding, alleged that the SIS and he himself had been involved in the kidnapping. Remias acted as a go-between for the agent, Oskar Fegyveres, and his family and reporters.

"We had certain suspicions over the death of Remias, and the latest development in the case gradually confirms these suspicions," Ivan Simko, a deputy chairman of the opposition Christian Democratic Movement, told Reuters.

"All I can say at the moment is that the explosive was probably set up in the car by a person who had an interest in eliminating Remias", said Kostov. "So far there is not sufficient information to accuse a concrete person."
Interior minister Ludovit Hudek, who was sacked last month, came under fire earlier this year over a controversial tape recording.
In it he appeared to be discussing firing a police investigator into the kidnapping with Ivan Lexa, a close Meciar ally who heads the SIS. The government said it was a fake.

Kovac Junior was dumped in Austria where authorities held him on an international warrant issued in Germany about an alleged fraud. A Vienna court refused to extradite him and said it believed the SIS had been involved in the kidnapping.
The SIS and Lexa have rejected the charges.

President Kovac is locked in a protracted power struggle with Meciar, whom he had helped oust in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in the spring of 1994, only to see Meciar re-elected later that year.
